forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: North Kesteven projects £533k general fund surplus as borrowing costs fall
news_drafts.lead: North Kesteven Council is projecting a General Fund surplus of £533,300 for 2026-27, driven mainly by lower-than-expected borrowing costs. The council budgeted for £2.54m in interest payments but now expects to spend only £1.92m, a saving of £617,600 built on timing of planned loan drawdowns for Lafford Homes development that concentrate borrowing into the second half of the year. Pay awards 0.3 percentage points higher than budgeted cost £51,400, and additional fuel costs add £22,800 of pressure. The surplus is being added to reserves: £233,300 to the Our Council Reserve and £300,000 to the Financial Resilience Reserve. The Housing Revenue Account, by contrast, projects a deficit of £160,700. The council is also managing capital scheme underspending of £1.8m against a budget of £10.1m, suggesting capital projects are not progressing at the pace anticipated in February.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Key Performance Indicator Exception Report Quarter 1 2026/27

findings.headline: 2025/26 Medium-Term Financial Strategy forecast balanced General Fund budgets through to 2027/28 but identified longer-term funding gaps.
findings.detail: The strategy anticipated a reduction of about £3.5m in business rates growth income from 2026/27, and identified uncertainty over New Homes Bonus. The five-workstream financial sustainability programme covers cost control, income growth, investment, and the use of reserves and external funding.
findings.matters: A council that forecasts balanced budgets while identifying longer-term gaps is a common pattern, and the business rates reduction is the specific income loss a peer would want to size.
findings.figures: Reduction of approximately £3.5m in business rates growth income from 2026/27
findings.quote: Although the 2025/26 Medium-Term Financial Strategy forecast balanced General Fund budgets through to 2027/28, it identified longer-term funding gaps.

findings.headline: The 2025/26 Medium-Term Financial Strategy forecast the Income Volatility Reserve at £10.3m at 31 March 2026, falling to £6.9m by 31 March 2027 and £4.0m by 31 March 2028.
findings.detail: These are forecasts from the 2025/26 Medium-Term Financial Strategy, and the paper does not state the actual 31 March 2026 balance. The paper notes that the planned reduction depends on delivering recurring savings and additional income rather than relying on reserves.
findings.matters: A reserve planned to fall by more than half over two years is a draw-down pattern finance directors at other councils will compare with their own.
findings.figures: £8.5m at 31 March 2025; £10.3m at 31 March 2026 (forecast); £6.9m at 31 March 2027 (forecast); £4.0m at 31 March 2028 (forecast)
findings.quote: forecast the reserve increasing from £8.5m at 31 March 2025 to £10.3m at 31 March 2026, before reducing to £6.9m at 31 March 2027 and £4.0m at 31 March 2028.

findings.headline: Council has reviewed the terms of its leisure services contract, with the leisure sector under pressure to deliver the financial return initially expected.
findings.detail: The paper says the leisure contract's financial performance is monitored alongside its effectiveness. It does not give the contract value or the outcome of the contractual review.
findings.matters: A council outsourcing leisure faces the same income pressure, and the contract review is a route other councils use when the expected return does not arrive.
findings.quote: the leisure sector under pressure to deliver the financial return initially expected

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing moved the Council's consumer grade from C3 to C2 in April 2026, and the auditor says the related significant weakness has been addressed.
findings.detail: The regulator's C2 grade records that some weaknesses remain in delivering the consumer standards. The paper says monthly review meetings with the regulator continue on the provider improvement plan.
findings.matters: A regulatory grade move and the auditor's closure of the related weakness are the two outcomes a lender and peer council would check against each other.
findings.quote: We are satisfied that the significant weakness in arrangements reported in 2025-26 has now been addressed

findings.headline: Bristol Arcade acquisition recorded at a cost of £40k, against a stand-alone valuation of £9.4k at 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: The auditor says the gap does not in isolation show a value for money concern, because the recorded rationale is wider development benefit. The auditor also says those benefits have not been shown as realised in the evidence reviewed, and identified no significant weakness in acquisition governance.
findings.matters: The gap between cost and valuation on a property bought for regeneration is a test finance officers elsewhere apply to their own acquisitions.
findings.quote: Its recorded cost of £40k exceeded its stand-alone valuation of £9.4k at 31 March 2026.
